name: The Tri-State Tornado
blurb: The longest tornado track ever recorded and the deadliest single tornado in United States history. It pre-dates the national database by twenty-five years, so this track is a reconstruction, not a survey.

name: Waco
blurb: An F5 through downtown Waco that killed 114, tied as the deadliest tornado in Texas history. Brick buildings on the town square fell into the street.

name: Flint — Beecher
blurb: An F5 through the Beecher area north of Flint on a Monday evening. 116 died, and it is still Michigan's deadliest tornado.

name: Worcester
blurb: A violent tornado across central Massachusetts the day after Flint. Ninety-four died, making it New England's deadliest.

name: Blackwell — Udall
blurb: Two F5s from the same storm after dark: Blackwell, Oklahoma, then Udall, Kansas. Udall's toll is still the deadliest of any Kansas tornado.

name: Ruskin Heights
blurb: An F5 from eastern Kansas into the south side of Kansas City, straight through the new Ruskin Heights subdivision. Forty-four died.

name: The 1965 Palm Sunday Outbreak
blurb: Violent tornadoes across six states in one afternoon and night, more than 250 dead. Every F4 and F5 of the day is here, with the tornadoes beside them.

name: Topeka
blurb: An F5 straight through the middle of Topeka, over Burnett's Mound, the hill local legend said would protect the city.

name: Charles City
blurb: An F5 through Charles City, one of two F5s in northeast Iowa that afternoon.

name: Lubbock
blurb: The tornado that produced the Fujita scale's first F5 rating and, by wrecking a city centre with engineered buildings in it, gave Ted Fujita the damage evidence the scale was built on.

name: The 1974 Super Outbreak
blurb: Thirty violent tornadoes in eighteen hours, six of them F5. Every F4 and F5 of the outbreak is here, with the tornadoes that ran alongside them.

name: Xenia
blurb: The Super Outbreak's signature tornado. It crossed Xenia in nine minutes, took half the town with it, and was filmed doing it.

name: Wichita Falls — Terrible Tuesday
blurb: An F4 through the south side of Wichita Falls at rush hour. Forty-two died, many of them in cars, which changed the advice on sheltering in a vehicle.

name: Grand Island
blurb: The Night of the Twisters. Seven tornadoes over one small city in three hours, three of them turning anticyclonically — backwards — which almost nothing does.

name: Barneveld
blurb: An F5 just after midnight that destroyed most of the village of Barneveld in minutes.

name: Niles — Wheatland
blurb: An F5 across the Ohio–Pennsylvania line on an evening nobody expected one: the outbreak that proved violent tornadoes happen east of the Plains.

name: Saragosa
blurb: Thirty dead in a town of four hundred. The warning went out in English to a community that largely spoke Spanish, and the lesson changed how warnings are issued.

name: Plainfield
blurb: The only F5 ever recorded in August, through Plainfield southwest of Chicago. No tornado warning was issued before it struck.

name: Andover
blurb: The Golden Spur trailer park, and one of the most filmed tornadoes of its era — the day that put storm chasing on the evening news.

name: Jarrell — Double Creek
blurb: It moved at walking pace and scoured the ground to bare subsoil. The slowest violent tornado on record, and the most complete destruction ever surveyed.

name: Oak Grove — Birmingham
blurb: An F5 at night through the western suburbs of Birmingham: Oak Grove, Rock Creek and Edgewater.

name: Bridge Creek — Moore
blurb: The fastest wind ever measured near the Earth's surface: 302 mph by mobile Doppler, 32 metres up, as it crossed Bridge Creek.

name: Mulhall
blurb: The same evening, further north, and by some measures the widest tornado ever sampled — its core flow wider than anything before or since.

name: Van Wert
blurb: A November F4 across northwest Ohio. The cinema manager moved his audience into the restrooms minutes before the auditorium was destroyed.

name: Hallam
blurb: About two and a half miles across, the widest tornado on record at the time. It all but erased the village of Hallam.

name: Greensburg
blurb: A 1.7-mile-wide tornado at night that destroyed about 95 percent of Greensburg: the first EF5 rated after the Enhanced Fujita scale took over that February.

name: Super Tuesday — Atkins
blurb: A 122-mile EF4 across Arkansas on the night of the presidential primaries, in an outbreak that killed 57 across the South.

name: Parkersburg — New Hartford
blurb: An EF5 on Memorial Day weekend that flattened about a third of Parkersburg, then crossed New Hartford.

name: Bowdle
blurb: A textbook wedge on the open Dakota prairie, in clear air, watched and filmed from close range for its whole life.

name: Wadena
blurb: A wide EF4 through Wadena on Minnesota's biggest tornado day on record.

name: Hackleburg — Phil Campbell
blurb: The deadliest tornado of the 2011 Super Outbreak: an EF5 on the ground for 132 miles from northwest Alabama into Tennessee.

name: The 2011 Super Outbreak
blurb: The largest tornado outbreak ever recorded. Every EF4 and EF5 of that day is here, with the tornadoes that ran alongside them.

name: Tuscaloosa — Birmingham
blurb: An EF4 shown live on television as it crossed Tuscaloosa and then the western suburbs of Birmingham. Sixty-four died.

name: Joplin
blurb: The deadliest single tornado since modern records began in 1950. It crossed a city of fifty thousand at its widest.

name: El Reno — Piedmont
blurb: Sixty-three miles from El Reno to Guthrie, EF5 for much of it. Two years before the other El Reno tornado, and a different storm entirely.

name: Henryville
blurb: An EF4 that destroyed much of Henryville, its school included, in the early March outbreak.

name: Moore
blurb: An EF5 through Moore fourteen years after the 1999 tornado crossed the same city. Twenty-four died, seven of them children at Plaza Towers Elementary.

name: El Reno
blurb: The widest tornado ever measured — 2.6 miles across — and the one that killed three experienced chasers, which changed how the field thinks about distance.

name: Washington
blurb: A November EF4 through Washington on a Sunday morning, one of the strongest late-season tornadoes the Midwest has seen.

name: Mayflower — Vilonia
blurb: An EF4 across Interstate 40 and through Vilonia, three years after another tornado hit the same town.

name: Pilger — the twins
blurb: Two EF4s side by side from one storm for nearly an hour, one of them through Pilger. Twin violent tornadoes are almost never seen.

name: Dayton — Memorial Day
blurb: An EF4 through the northern suburbs of Dayton near midnight on Memorial Day, one of sixteen tornadoes across the region in a single night.

name: Linwood
blurb: A wide EF4 across the Kansas River valley between Lawrence and Kansas City, after weeks of record rain. Nobody was killed.

name: Nashville — Cookeville
blurb: After midnight, an EF3 across downtown Nashville; an hour later the same storm dropped an EF4 on Cookeville that killed nineteen.

name: Bassfield — Soso
blurb: On Easter Sunday, an EF4 about two and a quarter miles wide, the widest ever recorded in Mississippi.

name: Mayfield — the Quad-State tornado
blurb: A hundred and sixty-eight miles on the ground in December, across four states, through the middle of Mayfield. Fifty-seven dead.

name: Rolling Fork — Silver City
blurb: Fifty-nine miles across the Mississippi Delta at nearly sixty miles an hour, through two small towns that had almost no time.

name: Little Rock
blurb: An EF3 through west and north Little Rock on a Friday afternoon, in an outbreak that also struck Wynne the same day.

name: Elkhorn — Blair
blurb: An EF4 through the northwestern edge of Omaha in the middle of the afternoon, in full view of half a city, with nobody killed.

name: Barnsdall
blurb: An EF4 late at night through Barnsdall and on toward Bartlesville.

name: Greenfield
blurb: Mobile radar measured winds between 309 and 318 mph inside it — among the highest ever recorded in a tornado — as it crossed the town.

name: The March 2025 outbreak
blurb: The first night of a three-day outbreak across the middle of the country, with long-track EF4s across northern Arkansas. Every EF4 of the night is here, with the tornadoes near them.

name: Somerset — London
blurb: A long-track EF4 across southeastern Kentucky near midnight, through the city of London.

name: Enderlin
blurb: The first EF5 rated anywhere in the United States since Moore in 2013, ending a twelve-year gap that had begun to look like a change in how the scale was being applied.
